analysis.one_liner: Limits bank overdraft fees to one per month and six per year, and bans fees on declined ATM and debit transactions.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee in July 2017 and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have set nationwide rules for overdraft fees, the charges banks collect when a customer spends more than is in their checking account. It would cap those fees at one per month and six per year, require that fees be reasonable and proportional to the amount overdrawn, ban nonsufficient-fund fees on ATM and debit card transactions, and require clear warnings before a customer triggers a fee. It also would have barred banks from reporting overdraft use to credit bureaus and frozen fee increases for one year while regulators wrote the rules [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who overdraw their checking accounts, who the bill's findings say bear the heaviest burden among low- and moderate-income account holders. A customer could no longer be charged multiple fees in a single day, repeated daily fees on one overdraft, or a fee caused by a temporary hold larger than the actual purchase. Anyone whose transaction would exceed the cap would be declined without a fee instead of charged [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low- and moderate-income checking account holders

how_it_helps.text: Caps overdraft coverage fees at one per calendar month and six per calendar year per account, ending repeat fees within a single day or month for the same shortfall [S3].
Requires fees to be reasonable and proportional to the size of the overdraft, and directs the consumer bureau to set a presumptively reasonable fee amount with the banking regulators [S3].

Banks could no longer charge a nonsufficient-fund fee on any ATM or debit card transaction, and could not charge an overdraft fee when the overdraft came only from a debit hold larger than the actual purchase [S3].

Consumers must be warned at the ATM or teller when a transaction would trigger a fee and given the chance to cancel it, and banks must post transactions in an order that avoids avoidable overdraft fees [S3].

Overdraft fees must be disclosed as an annual percentage rate so customers can compare them to other credit options, and banks may not report negative overdraft information to credit bureaus when the overdraft is repaid under the program [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Banks and credit unions that collect overdraft and nonsufficient-fund fees would lose a large share of that revenue. The bill's findings describe institutions collecting a high flat fee on every overdraft, sometimes several in one day, so the cap on frequency and the reasonableness requirement directly cut into that income [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Banks and credit unions collecting overdraft fees

drawbacks.text: Customers who exceed the caps would no longer have their transactions covered: the bill lets the bank decline to pay the overdraft without charging a fee, so a purchase could be rejected at the register, which supporters of the current system argue is a real cost for some consumers [S3].

Banks and credit unions argue that overdraft coverage is a service that lets small transactions go through, and that capping fees could lead institutions to decline more transactions, close the accounts of frequent overdrawers, or raise other account fees to make up lost revenue. The bill's one-year moratorium on fee increases temporarily limits that adjustment for existing fees, but does not bar banks from raising other fees after the rules take effect [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protections are concrete and the cost falls almost entirely on the fee-collecting institutions, not on taxpayers. The main honest trade-off is that heavy overdraft users could see more transactions declined once they hit the cap, and banks might recoup revenue through other account charges over time. On balance, the bill would shift money from fee revenue back to the account holders least able to pay it.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Financial Services Committee, which never took it up, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Carolyn Maloney introduced the bill on July 28, 2017, joined by Rep. Keith Ellison as an original cosponsor [S1][S3].
The House referred it to the Committee on Financial Services the day it was introduced [S5].
The action history shows no further steps: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S1][S5].
Ten House members — Maloney, Ellison, and eight cosponsors, all Democrats — supported the bill, but the committee that would have to move it never scheduled action on it [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks and credit unions are better off because the bill died: they kept collecting high flat overdraft fees on every covered transaction, including multiple fees in one day and daily fees on lingering overdrafts, with no cap on frequency and no reasonableness standard [S3].

for.name: Rep. Carolyn Maloney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Overdraft Protection Act of 2017 in the House.

for.name: Rep. Keith Ellison
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor when the bill was introduced.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee (Chair Jeb Hensarling)
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over banking bills
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill sat with no further action until the Congress ended.

against.name: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau under Acting Director Mick Mulvaney
against.what_they_did: Backed away from the bureau's own pending overdraft-fee rulemaking, easing pressure on banks that a parallel regulatory crackdown might have created.

sides.party_line_note: All ten supporters — the sponsor, the original cosponsor, and eight additional cosponsors — were House Democrats, and the Republican-led Financial Services Committee never brought the bill up.

industries.note: Overdraft and nonsufficient-fund fees are a major direct charge on customers, and the bill's own findings describe institutions collecting a high flat fee on every overdraft, sometimes several in a single day, with the burden falling on low- and moderate-income consumers [S3]. Capping fees at one per month and six per year, requiring them to be proportional to the overdraft, and banning fees on declined ATM and debit transactions would cut directly into that revenue stream [S3]. The institutions' interest in keeping the fees runs against the account holders who pay them.
